docs.title: Xerces Chess Engine
docs.text: Xerces is a self-learning chess engine combining Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with a neural network policy/value model trained via self-play.

docs.title: What is Xerces?
docs.text: Xerces is an open-source chess engine built around Monte Carlo Tree Search and a custom-trained neural network. It is a personal project, built and trained on a single consumer GPU (RTX 2080, i9-9700K) by one person (so far).

docs.title: Is Xerces an Lc0 clone or fork?
docs.text: No, I wrote the C++ and python myself from scratch. Interestingly though, the chess-library backend was provided by Disservin, the lead developer of Stockfish.

docs.title: Why build this instead of just using Stockfish or LC0?
docs.text: I've been interested in chess and chess engines for a long time and the best way for me to see how things work is to build it myself. It's also fun to be able to experiment with new ideas on my own project.

docs.title: How strong is it?
docs.text: I estimate around 3300 Elo (human scale) based on validation runs against Stockfish at fixed depth (12, 15, 20 plies, etc). In competition mode it runs 5-6 centipawn loss on average.

docs.title: How does it do against Stockfish?
docs.text: Xerces is validated against Stockfish every 10 model retrains, in paired games from UHO openings (each position played as both colors). It is currently scoring ~0.4/1.0 against Stockfish 17.1 at depth 15.

docs.title: Why train on a single GPU instead of cloud compute?
docs.text: That's intentional. Part of the appeal of the project is the constraint — figuring out how much strength you can get out of a limited hardware budget is more interesting than throwing resources at the problem. The design decisions throughout the stack (efficient board encoding, aggressive caching, adaptive early stopping, prior fudging) all exist because compute is tight.

docs.title: Do you use history planes?
docs.text: Yes, as of the current primary architecture. Xerces started from the opposite hypothesis — that AlphaZero-style history planes are largely cargo cult, with the model learning to ignore most of them. That was tested head-to-head against a history-aware encoding, and stacking a short window of prior positions turned out to earn its keep, so it's now the primary encoding rather than a side experiment. The current scheme stacks the current position plus 5 prior frames (6 total), each in the same token-per-square style as the base encoding, alongside a per-frame repetition flag and a few metadata scalars (castling rights, side to move, halfmove clock). It's a lighter touch than the classic 8-ply AZ history stack — full board planes per frame — while still giving the model direct access to recent piece trajectories and repetitions instead of relying solely on the search tree for that signal.

docs.title: What's different about the board encoding?
docs.text:
Rather than binary piece-plane stacks, Xerces's base encoding represents a position as 64 integer tokens — one per square — always from the side-to-move's perspective. The primary model stacks 6 of these frames (current position + 5 prior) rather than just one — see "Do you use history planes?" above. A few design choices worth noting:

  • Castling rights are folded into the king token (9 possible values) in the single-frame encoding, rather than using separate planes.
  • The en passant target square receives a dedicated token directly on that square, giving the model spatial context about which file is eligible.
  • The board is always flipped so the side to move appears as "white," so the model never has to learn two perspectives of the same position — history frames stay frozen to that same orientation too, so they remain spatially aligned with the current frame.

docs.title: How fast does it run?
docs.text: On the RTX 2080, the ~18.4M parameter m137_8c8t network is served in fp16 through ONNX Runtime + TensorRT. With the MCTSForest batching leaf encoding across all active games, selfplay sustains around 40,000 leaves per second, of which roughly 21,000 per second actually reach the network. The gap is absorbed before inference: the C++ priors cache resolves repeated positions, terminal nodes need no evaluation, and matelock's must-visit leaves are forced without a fresh prediction. That works out to roughly 750 games per hour of training; validation vs Stockfish is about 100 games per hour.

docs.title: Why the name Xerces?
docs.text: Mostly because I think its cool!

docs.title: What's next for the project?
docs.text: More selfplay. I think the better data -> better search -> better model -> better data loop is still progressing (slowly). Beyond that, the rescoring pipeline continues to be tuned as the model improves.

docs.title: What's the biggest thing you've learned building this?
docs.text:
1. Confidently wrong priors are much much worse than noisy but useful priors.
  2. Managing side-to-move (STM) perspective flipping is the hardest part of the whole project.
  3. Stockfish and Leela are hard to beat.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Xerces is split across two repositories. pyfastchess is a C++ Python extension that owns board representation, the MCTS tree, and position caching. chessbot is the Python package that owns neural network inference, training orchestration, rescoring, and tooling.

chessbot (Python)
  run_selfplay.py       orchestrator — workers, retrain loop, validation
  GameLooper            batched NN inference, concurrent game management
  Rescorer              SF analysis, blunder detection, training data prep
  retrain_worker.py     model training subprocess
  GameViewer            game replay and review tools
  model.py              network architecture definitions
  infer_ort_trt.py      ONNX Runtime + TensorRT inference backend

pyfastchess (C++ extension)
  MCTSTree              PUCT selection, backprop, early stopping hooks
  MCTSNode              per-node state, visit counts, WDL accumulators
  Backend (Board)       board state, move gen, 64-token encoding
  Cache                 LRU priors cache, raw policy cache

Pages in this section:

  • Stack Overview — how Python and C++ are layered; the chess-library backend stub
  • Search — MCTS in C++: node structure, PUCT selection, caches
  • Neural Network — m137_8c8t model, ONNX Runtime + TensorRT inference
  • Selfplay Suite — SelfPlayRunner, GameLooper, StockfishThread, game curriculum
  • Rescoring & Retraining — SF analysis pipeline, training data prep, retrain subprocess
  • Review Tools — GameViewer, RecordKeeper

docs.title: Rescoring Overview
docs.text: After a game finishes, it isn't used for training directly. The raw selfplay data contains noisy outcome labels and visit distributions that reflect the current (imperfect) model. The Rescorer processes each finished game asynchronously, runs Stockfish analysis on every position, and builds cleaner training targets before anything reaches the training queue.

docs.title: SF Analysis Pipeline
docs.text: Each game pickle contains the full move history and per-ply NN outputs. Rescorer.start_game() iterates through the plies and submits positions to the Stockfish queue for analysis. Results come back asynchronously via handle_sf_result(), which stores the best move, centipawn evaluation, and WDL triple for each ply. Every position gets full analysis — an earlier position-keyed cache (SFCache) that skipped re-analysis of repeated positions was tried and removed; it wasn't paying off.

docs.title: Training Targets
docs.text:
The value target for each ply is a blended 3-component WDL:

Y = 0.5 * z_wdl + 0.5 * sf_wdl

where z_wdl is the game result converted to WDL and sf_wdl is Stockfish's WDL at that ply. When SF analysis is unavailable, the target falls back to z_wdl alone. Blending the outcome with Stockfish's read keeps the target grounded in what actually happened while pulling it toward a stronger positional signal — an earlier variant also mixed in the MCTS search WDL, but that component was dropped.

docs.title: Blunder Handling
docs.text:
After SF analysis is complete, finalize_game() scores every ply by centipawn loss against Stockfish's best move. The blunder threshold depends on the outcome: it is stricter for the side that went on to lose or draw than for the side that won. Each ply's policy target is the raw search visit distribution, with every legal move floored at one visit. What happens next depends on how bad the move was:

  • Below the blunder threshold: the ply trains on its own visits, unmodified. There is no Stockfish blending in the band between "equivalent" and "blunder"; search is trusted there.
  • True blunder: the ply is sent to the LC0 teacher, and the teacher's samples replace Xerces's own for that position (see LC0 Teacher below). A true blunder is one that crosses the threshold and didn't still leave the mover clearly winning.
  • Blunder the teacher can't take (e.g. the position has castling rights): the visit policy is blended toward a Stockfish point mass on its best move. The blend strengthens with the size of the loss. If the mover won the game anyway, the blend is skipped, and the model is trusted over Stockfish.

docs.title: Blunder Replay Pool (BRP)
docs.text:
Fixing a blunder in the training data doesn't prove the model stopped making it. The blunder replay pool tracks the positions where Xerces actually went wrong and keeps re-testing them as the model trains.

Admission. After rescoring, each ply is checked against a small set of candidate rules, all requiring that the mover then drew or lost the game:

  • a balanced position thrown away by a large centipawn loss
  • a clearly better position played into equality or worse
  • a winning position given back
  • a decisive or mating advantage squandered

Only games traceable from the standard start position or a book line qualify (startpos, UHO, the opening books and validation games), because the position is rebuilt by replaying the move history. Before a candidate is admitted, the LC0 teacher is asked about it. If the teacher answers cleanly, the blunder is correctable rather than an artifact of Stockfish's search horizon, and it joins the pool with the teacher's move banked as a target.

Probing. Every tenth retrain runs a bulk BRP round: up to a quarter of the pool is replayed. Positions are drawn on recency of their last probe, so each one gets a rest between challenges. Each probe is a fresh Xerces search from the blunder position, and its move is scored by Stockfish:

  • Pass: Xerces finds the best move or one within a small equivalence margin. The position is evicted as solved.
  • Fail: the position stays in the pool. Stockfish's budget for that position rises on each failure until a deep, cached evaluation locks in the best move, so repeat probes become cheaper and more reliable.
  • Third fail: the position is escalated to the LC0 teacher, which plays it out and contributes training samples (see LC0 Teacher below).
  • Past five fails: the position is retired, which keeps the pool from filling with positions the current model can't learn yet.

Pass rates, fail depths and positions that keep failing are logged per round, which gives a direct read on whether the model is actually learning from its mistakes, independent of the validation ladder.

docs.title: Collar Rescoring
docs.text: The eval collar tracks consecutive plies where one side's evaluation stays above a threshold. When the collar fires, it retroactively adjusts the game result label for the affected stretch of plies, overriding the final game outcome with the collar evaluation. This corrects for cases where a clearly winning position was eventually drawn or lost due to adjudication noise or model error, keeping the value targets honest about who was winning at each point in the game.

docs.title: Sample Acceptance
docs.text:
Every position from a game trains unless its sample goes to the LC0 teacher instead (true blunders), or the ply was flagged to skip training at game time. When a position goes to the teacher through a stream that still keeps the xc0 sample (policy/value misses, pool candidates), that xc0 sample trains at half weight and the teacher's samples at full.

KL boosting. On plies where the played move was sound, positions where search disagreed sharply with the network's first guess get more weight. The KL divergence between prior and visits is tracked as running median and 80th-percentile estimates. Plies above either mark have their policy weight multiplied up, and the same is done for the value weight using a value-side KL. This reweights informative positions rather than filtering anything out.

docs.title: LC0 Teacher
docs.text:
Stockfish can say a move was a mistake, but its single best move is a thin policy target. For positions where Xerces is known to go wrong, a Leela network acts as a search teacher. A dedicated lc0 worker runs the network through the same ORT+TensorRT machinery as selfplay (the lc0_trt backend) and plays a short probe from the flagged position, currently 3 plies of full MCTS. Every ply it plays becomes a training sample: straight visit distribution and WDL, at full weight. The teacher's moves and visits are mapped into Xerces's 1858 move domain (lc0_utils).

Positions reach the teacher through a few streams, all on one queue and deduplicated per ply:

  • True blunders. A ply Stockfish rates as a real blunder is sent to the teacher instead of training on Xerces's own (wrong) visits. The xc0 sample is dropped.
  • Blunder replay escalations. Positions from the blunder replay pool that Xerces keeps failing are escalated to the teacher (see below).
  • Policy/value misses. A ply that wasn't a true blunder but still lost meaningful ground, where Stockfish's move sits outside Xerces's top candidates by visits or by prior, or where the prior liked it and search didn't. The xc0 sample still trains here, at half weight, alongside the teacher's.

Teacher samples are collected in their own lc0_buffer and flushed as pure-lc0 shards. The retrain draw gives these shards priority, so the corrected signal reaches the model quickly instead of being diluted across the whole buffer. Positions with castling rights are skipped, because lc0 and Xerces index castling moves differently. The teacher is entirely optional: with no lc0 model configured, no lc0 worker is spawned and rescoring runs on Stockfish alone.

docs.title: Retraining
docs.text:
Retraining runs in a fresh process (retrain_worker.py) spawned for each cycle and torn down afterwards. On an 8GB GPU, selfplay inference and training can't share VRAM comfortably; a process that exits releases all of its GPU memory, so workers always resume on a clean slate.

The buffers. Rescored samples accumulate in a live buffer and are written out as fixed-size shards into three tiers:

  • Primary: fresh selfplay shards not yet trained on, plus the pure-lc0 teacher shards.
  • Replay: primary shards that have already been through one retrain.
  • Historic: a read-only slice of the bootstrap corpus (lc0 and early Xerces data). It anchors the model to the pretraining distribution and can be drawn again and again.

The draw. A retrain fires when the primary tier fills up. Each retrain draws a fixed mix of 12 primary + 12 replay + 4 historic shards. The primary draw reserves slots for lc0 teacher shards (two when several are waiting, one otherwise), so teacher corrections land within a retrain or two of being produced. After a successful retrain, the trained primary shards rotate into replay and the replay shards that were drawn are discarded. Every selfplay sample therefore trains exactly twice: once fresh, once as replay.

The cycle.

  1. The worker loads the shards and, before training, runs the current model over held-out slices of primary (pure xc0), historic and lc0 data. These predictions become the per-epoch validation metrics, scored on data the model has never trained on.
  2. It shuffles primary records across shard boundaries, mixes in replay and historic, and tells the orchestrator it is ready.
  3. The orchestrator pauses selfplay. The worker waits until every selfplay worker confirms it has released its GPU sessions (with a timeout backstop), then allocates and trains.
  4. Training is a single pass with AdamW (decoupled weight decay on matrix and conv weights only; biases, norm gains and PReLU slopes are exempt), fp16 autocast and gradient clipping. The AdamW moments and the GradScaler state persist across retrains, so the optimizer behaves like one continuous run rather than restarting cold every cycle. Weights are used directly; there is no EMA of the player.
  5. On completion, the orchestrator rebuilds the TRT engine, unpauses selfplay on the new weights, and only then aggregates the validation metrics. Workers are never kept waiting on bookkeeping.

The retrain view shows per-epoch metrics:

  • value CE — cross-entropy of the model's WDL predictions against the blended training targets.
  • value correlation — Pearson correlation between predicted and target scalar values (win - loss). Tracks whether the model's ordinal ranking of positions improves even when absolute calibration is noisy.
  • policy CE — cross-entropy of policy logits against the rescored visit distribution targets.
  • top-1 accuracy — fraction of positions where the model's top policy move matches the training target's top move.
  • CE gain vs uniform — policy CE improvement over a uniform distribution baseline, measuring how much the model has learned to concentrate probability on good moves.

docs.title: Board Encoding
docs.text:
The base building block is a single position encoded as 64 integer tokens, one per square, always from the perspective of the side to move (STM-as-white). Black positions are flipped via sq ^ 56 before encoding so the model always sees its own pieces as the "white" side.

Single-frame token values:

Range Meaning 0 Empty square 1–5 STM pieces: pawn, knight, bishop, rook, queen 6–9 STM king with castling rights: none, kingside, queenside, both 10–18 Opponent pieces (same structure, +9 offset) 19 En passant target square

Castling rights are folded into the king token in this single-frame encoding — no separate planes are needed. The en passant square gets its own token on the target square, giving the model direct spatial context about which file is eligible. Vocabulary size is 21. This encoding is defined in C++ (pyfastchess) and is fixed across the entire stack.

The primary model encoding (xc0h) stacks 6 of these frames — the current position plus 5 prior positions, oldest padded if the game is younger than that — instead of just the current one. Each frame uses a simplified per-square token (pieces 1-6/7-12 by ownership, no castling folded in, EP token, pad token for missing history), all frozen to the same STM-relative orientation so frames stay spatially aligned across time. The stack is followed by a per-frame repetition flag and 3 metadata scalars (combined castling rights, side to move, halfmove clock), for a flat length of K*64 + K + 3 — 393 tokens at history_K=6. This was adopted as the primary architecture after testing showed it outperforming the single-frame, no-history version (see the FAQ: "Do you use history planes?").

docs.title: m137_8c8t Architecture
docs.text:
The active model is m137_8c8t (registry key m13-7-8c8t-d256, built by build_pt_expandy_swiglu in src/chessbot/model.py): 8 conv blocks followed by 8 transformer blocks at width D = 256, ~18.4M parameters, reading the xc0h history encoding above. It is a PyTorch model trained under fp16 autocast. LayerNorm is used throughout (an experimental L1.5 norm is available via cfg["norm"]); there is no BatchNorm, since small, variable selfplay batches make it unstable.

xc0h stem. Each of the 6 history frames is embedded per square with an 18-d token embedding (15-token vocab). The embedding table is initialized compositionally rather than randomly: every piece row is side + movement primitive (us/them plus pawn, knight, diagonal, orthogonal, king), so a queen starts as diagonal + orthogonal, and the EP token starts as empty + them. The 6 frames are concatenated per square (108 channels) alongside the per-frame repetition flags, a castling-rights embedding (16 states → one learned value per square), side to move and the halfmove clock, each scalar with its own learnable scale. A linear projection + LayerNorm maps this to D - 4 = 252 channels, and 4 fixed spatial planes (ones, checkerboard, rank, file) are appended after the norm so it cannot flatten their geometry. Each plane has a learnable scale so the convs can mute any that aren't useful. The result is a [B, 256, 8, 8] grid.

Conv stack (8 blocks). All conv blocks are prenorm residual blocks over the 8×8 grid, so local spatial structure resolves before any attention runs.

  • 2 plain blocks: LN → Conv3×3 → act → Conv3×3 → act, added back to the input.
  • 6 gated expandy blocks: each half of the block is a depthwise-separable-style factorization: a grouped 3×3 conv (4 groups) that expands D → 2D, then a 1×1 pointwise conv back down to D. This buys a wide 512-channel intermediate at a fraction of a dense 3×3's cost. Between the two halves, a 1×1 conv + sigmoid produces a per-square, per-channel gate that multiplies the block's output before the residual add, so each block can choose, square by square, how much it writes into the stream.

Learnable PReLUs. Every conv activation is a per-channel PReLU. Slopes initialize at 0.03, which makes them exactly the LeakyReLU(0.03) they replaced, so grafting onto an older leaky checkpoint is lossless. They are clamped to [-0.5, 0.5] after every optimizer step (project_params), which keeps any channel from drifting into a linear or sign-flipping regime.

Positions and global accumulators. The grid is flattened to 64 square tokens and a learned positional embedding is added, scaled by a learnable pos_scale. 8 learned global tokens are then appended, giving a [B, 72, 256] sequence. These are the model's read-out registers: after the trunk, every output head reads from dedicated accumulator tokens instead of pooling the board.

Token Read by 64, 65, 66 Win, draw and loss heads 67 SmartGate 68 SmartGate and both policy towers (shared) 69 Both policy towers 70 From tower only 71 To tower only

Transformer trunk (8 blocks). All blocks are prenorm: LN → MHA (8 heads) → residual, then LN → FFN → residual. The K projection has no bias, since softmax is shift-invariant per query and a K bias would be dead weight.

  • Blocks 1–4 (FF): GELU feed-forward, 256 → 1024 → 256.
  • Blocks 5–8 (SwiGLU): down(SiLU(gate(x)) * up(x)) with a 1024-wide hidden layer, plus tanh-gated attention. The attention output is multiplied by 1 + tanh(g(x)), where g is a per-token, per-channel linear map. The gate ranges over (0, 2), so it can both suppress and boost what each token takes from attention. g is zero-initialized, so the gate is exactly 1 at init and the block starts as plain attention.

Dropout in the trunk is stochastic per site: each attention/FFN dropout site is switched on independently with a set duty probability (set_dropout) rather than always running. A final LayerNorm closes the trunk.

Value head (tokens 64–66). Win, draw and loss each get an independent head on their own accumulator: Linear(256 → 64) → GELU → Linear(64 → 1). The three outputs form the WDL logits, trained as a 3-class softmax, STM-POV.

Policy head: from/to attention. Two towers build a 256-d "from" and "to" vector per square. Each tower takes the 64 squares plus its accumulators (68, 69, and 70 or 71), applies a GELU projection residual, then runs a 4-head attention in which the squares query over the squares and the accumulators, followed by an output residual. Move logits are the dot products of the normalized from/to vectors, scaled by 1/sqrt(256), giving a 64×64 from-to matrix. Queen, rook and bishop promotions get their own logits: the rank-7 → rank-8 sub-block of that matrix plus small per-piece promo_from/promo_to projections. A knight promotion uses the plain from → to slot. Only the 1858 sometimes-legal move slots (build_sometimes_legal_mask) are emitted; C++ scatters them back into the 4288 flat space.

SmartGate: a learned legality veto. In parallel, the gate reads tokens 67 and 68 concatenated (512-d) through a GELU FFN (512 → 1024 → 512) with a residual and LayerNorm, then a linear layer to one shut-logit per move slot (1858). The policy output is

policy = move_logits - scale * sigmoid(gate_raw)

Because the subtracted term is always ≥ 0, the gate is suppress-only: it can push a move down but never invent one. Both knobs are learnable and clamped after every step. The per-move bias lives in [0, 5] and starts at 4.0 (sigmoid(4) ≈ 0.98, mostly shut). The global scale lives in [0, 12] and starts at 1.0. At init the gate therefore applies a near-uniform shift that softmax ignores, and it earns its scale as it learns legality.

Gate loss. The gate has its own supervised objective: a BCE on gate_raw predicting illegality, with any move the policy target gives visits to counted as legal (every legal move carries a 1-visit floor). Legal moves are up-weighted 5× and the weights are renormalized per position. The gate loss is held at 5% of the main (policy + value) loss. Once it falls below 5.0 its share shrinks proportionally, so a well-trained gate stops competing with the main objective.

Diagnostics. In training, the model can track hotspot statistics (peak activations and where they occur) at the policy dot products, the FFN and SwiGLU down-projections, and the residual stream. It also keeps 500-step EMAs of gate mean, spread and range for both the conv gates and the attention gates. These feed the gate-health readout in the retrain logs and add no host syncs outside print cadence.

The value used elsewhere (nn_value) is derived in C++ as win - loss. Policy post-processing — softmax over legal moves, uniform_eps blending, prior_clip_max clamping — is handled in C++ (build_priors) after raw logits are inserted into the raw cache.

docs.title: ONNX Runtime + TensorRT Inference
docs.text:
Inference runs through ONNX Runtime with the TensorRT execution provider (src/chessbot/infer_ort_trt.py), the ort_trt backend. TensorFlow has been removed from the active path (old Keras/TF architectures are quarantined in legacy_models.py).

After each retrain, prepare_trt() exports the current TorchScript model to ONNX (export_ts_to_onnx, input enc_in: [B, 393] int64 for xc0h) and stages it in the run's TRT cache. Workers then call make_ort_trt_infer(), which builds an ORT InferenceSession with:

  • TensorrtExecutionProvider — fp16 enabled, 4 GB workspace, fixed shape profile (enc_in:1x393 min, {max_bs}x393 opt/max). Compiled engines are cached to disk keyed by the sha256[:12] of the ONNX bytes, so subsequent sessions load the engine instead of paying the multi-minute compile. TRT is required, not a fallback — the session raises if it doesn't come up on TRT.

infer(pair) casts the board batch to int64, runs the session for policy_logits and value_out, and softmaxes the WDL logits on the CPU, returning (logits [B, 1858], wdl [B, 3]). pt_eager (raw PyTorch) remains available for debugging and as the retrain backend; both expose the same (logits, wdl) interface, so the selfplay loop is inference-backend-agnostic.

A third backend, lc0_trt, swaps in a distilled Leela network over the same TRT machinery — see the rescoring pipeline for how LC0 is used as a distillation teacher.

docs.title: Review Tools
docs.text: Every game is serialized to a pickle containing the full move history, per-ply search stats, NN outputs, and Stockfish analysis results. The review tools load these pickles for post-hoc analysis.

docs.title: GameViewer
docs.text:
GameViewer is the primary analysis tool. It loads a game pickle and provides a per-ply breakdown of everything that happened during search.

For each move, the view shows:

  • Visit counts — how many simulations visited each candidate move.
  • Policy prior vs search distribution — the raw NN prior alongside the final visit share, making it easy to see where search agreed with or diverged from the network's initial guess.
  • Q and Qema — mean action value and its exponential moving average, both surfaced per candidate.
  • PUCT contributions — the Q and U components broken out, so you can see whether a move was selected for its value or because it was underexplored.
  • Entropy and KL divergence — visit distribution entropy and KL from the prior, measuring how much the search reshaped the policy over the course of the simulation budget.
  • Stockfish comparison — the SF best move and centipawn evaluation from post-hoc analysis, shown alongside the Xerces move for each ply.

seek_cpl(threshold) jumps to the next ply where centipawn loss exceeds a threshold, making it fast to navigate to the most instructive moments in a game.

docs.title: LC0 Comparison
docs.text: GameViewer can run Leela Chess Zero on any position and overlay its policy distribution alongside Xerces. This surfaces distribution differences and KL divergence between the two engines' policies — useful for examining how Xerces weights moves relative to a well-established reference engine, and for spotting systematic gaps in opening knowledge or positional understanding.

docs.title: Deeper Stockfish Evaluation
docs.text: The rescoring pipeline runs Stockfish at a fixed depth for training data generation. During review, any position can be re-evaluated to an arbitrary depth directly from GameViewer. This is useful when the standard rescoring depth was shallow on a particular position and you want a stronger ground-truth evaluation to assess whether the engine's play was sound.

docs.title: RecordKeeper
docs.text: RecordKeeper aggregates game outcomes and performance metrics across the worker pool. It tracks W/D/L totals, total simulations used, active game counts, and throughput — moves per second, leafs per second, batch fill rate, and cache hit rate. These metrics feed the live telemetry display during a run and are also logged to the progress CSV for offline analysis.

docs.title: MCTS Overview
docs.text: Xerces uses Monte Carlo Tree Search with PUCT selection, implemented entirely in C++ inside pyfastchess. The Python side submits leaf nodes for NN evaluation and calls back with results; everything else — descent, virtual loss, backpropagation, caching — is handled in C++.

docs.title: Node Structure
docs.text:
Each MCTSNode holds:

  • Visit count (N) — atomic, incremented during virtual loss and resolved on backprop.
  • WDL accumulators (p_win, p_draw, p_loss) — cumulative sums of backpropped WDL values (white-POV). Q = (p_win - p_loss) / N.
  • Qema — exponential moving average of Q. Span is configurable (qema_span, default 40). Used in robust selection to smooth noisy early estimates.
  • Qdelta_sign — EMA of the sign of Q deltas relative to the parent's STM POV; positive means Q has been trending in favor of the side to move. Span is configurable (qdelta_span, default 100). Used to detect Q convergence in early stopping.
  • Children (ordered_children) — vector of ChildEntry structs with uci, prior (post-fudge), raw_prior, and a lazily-allocated unique_ptr<MCTSNode>. Children are only allocated when first selected.
  • State flags — is_expanded, is_pending, is_inflight, is_terminal.
  • Visit share — EMA tracking how often this child is selected relative to its siblings.

docs.title: PUCT Selection
docs.text:
The selection formula is standard PUCT:

U = c_puct * prior * sqrt(parent_N) / (1 + child_N)
score = Q_eff + U

Q_eff applies contempt adjustment on top of the raw Q value. Unvisited children initialize with FPU reduction: Q_parent - fpu_reduction, discouraging immediate exploration of all children.

Selection is pruned based on the remaining simulation budget: the tree skips children whose prior falls below a threshold determined by pruning_factor, concentrating visits on the most promising moves.

docs.title: Sharp Move Boost
docs.text:
Captures and checks are where a policy net most often under-rates a move. The sharp boost guarantees them a look without touching the priors. While a node's visit count is inside sharp_window ([100, 250]), each sharp child (one that is a capture, a check, or both) gets an extra exploration term:

U += u_scale * sharp_boost * sharp * max(0, 1 - N/sharp_M) / (1 + N)

sharp is capture + check (0–2), so a capturing check gets double. The bonus decays linearly to zero by sharp_M visits (10), so it only lifts moves the search has barely explored and then gets out of the way. Live settings are sharp_boost: 0.05 and sharp_M: 10.0.

  • Priors run unencumbered first. Below 100 visits the node searches on plain PUCT. The boost only checks, once the node is established, that sharp moves got a few visits.
  • Additive, not multiplicative. A multiplier on the prior can't be tuned across the prior range (3× of 0.001 is still nothing), so the bonus is added to the prior term.
  • Applies at any depth, keyed on each node's own visit count. Sharp flags are tagged lazily, once per node, the first time it enters the window. They are not stored in the cache.
  • Boosted visits are kept out of training. Each child counts the visits the boost decided (boosted_N), and these are subtracted before the visit distribution becomes a policy target. The net is never trained to imitate the boost itself.

Telemetry reports how often the boost changed a selection (sharp= on the PUCT stats line), a per-move sharp_by_depth histogram, and per-candidate boosted counts in game records. In a live sweep (~1,700 games per arm), sharp_boost 0.05 cut selfplay CPL from 7.07 to 6.54 versus no boost. A follow-up sweep over sharp_M (5, 10, 20) was flat.

If a forced mate is detected anywhere in the tree, the node sets a must_visit_uci flag via an atomic state machine, overriding PUCT to steer all remaining visits toward the mating line.

docs.title: Leaf Collection
docs.text:
collect_many_leaves(n_new, n_fastpath) is the main interface Python calls each inference batch. It runs PUCT descent up to n_new + n_fastpath times and categorizes the results:

  • New leaf — node not yet expanded; board position and Zobrist key returned to Python for NN evaluation.
  • Cache hit — node found in the priors cache; value applied immediately without Python involvement, counted toward n_fastpath.
  • Terminal — checkmate, stalemate, 50-move rule, or repetition draw; resolved with a hard WDL without NN.

Python only sees new leaves. Cache hits and terminals are handled entirely in C++.

docs.title: Backpropagation
docs.text: After apply_result(node, priors, wdl) is called, WDL values are backpropped along the path from the expanded leaf to the root. Each ancestor accumulates the WDL and recomputes Q. Virtual loss is removed at the same time.

docs.title: Priors Cache
docs.text:
The priors cache is a 1-million-entry LRU map keyed on the 64-bit Zobrist hash. Each entry stores:

  • The post-softmax policy priors (uci, prior) for all legal moves at that position
  • The original NN WDL (white-POV)
  • The scalar value (win - loss)
  • The visit count at the time the entry was written

On a cache hit during descent, the tree expands the node using the stored priors and WDL immediately, then backprops — no NN call needed. The hit rate is tracked and surfaced in telemetry.

docs.title: Raw Policy Cache
docs.text:
A secondary cache stores raw (Zobrist, value, policy_logits) tuples, inserted in bulk by Python after each NN inference batch via raw_cache_bulk_insert_np(). This feeds the priors cache on the C++ side: when the tree needs priors for a node, it checks the raw cache first, applies softmax, uniform_eps, and prior_clip_max in C++ (build_priors), and stores the result in the priors cache. Optionally, priors that are still too spread out after that are sharpened further — see Prior Temperature Scaling.

The separation allows Python to insert raw logits once per batch and let C++ handle post-processing, keeping the interface thin.

docs.title: Tree Reuse
docs.text: When a move is played, advance_root(move_uci) promotes the chosen child to be the new root. The subtree rooted at that child is preserved — all its accumulated visits, WDL, and cached priors carry over into the next search. Subtrees for other moves are discarded. Tree reuse is configurable and is on by default.

docs.title: Python-Side Extensions
docs.text:
MCTSTree in mcts_utils.py extends the C++ fasttree with Python-side logic:

  • Simulation scheduling — sim budget is set per-ply from a dict schedule (e.g., ramp from 1000 at ply 0 to 2800 at ply 45).
  • Effort scaling — on top of the ply schedule, each move's sims floor and ceiling are multiplied by a scale from an effort table. The table was built offline from ~200k training games by measuring how often an outcome-changing mistake happens in each bin of game phase × |parent Q| × parent draw probability. Bins where Xerces plays worse get more sims; quiet, low-stakes bins get fewer. Scales are clamped to [0.5×, 2×], so the budget moves to where mistakes actually happen rather than growing overall. effort_alpha sets how strongly the measured mistake rates are turned into scales (0 = flat).
  • Early stopping — checks every es_check_every sims using two criteria: robust selection confidence (RSC) and Jensen-Shannon divergence stability of the visit distribution. When either is met, the search stops before the ceiling.
  • Move sampling — after search completes, the move to play is sampled from the top-5 candidates using temperature that decays linearly from ply 0 to ply 30.
  • Dirichlet noise — added to root priors once per move to encourage exploration.

docs.title: Two-Repo Structure
docs.text:
Xerces is built across two repositories that are developed and versioned independently.

pyfastchess is a C++ Python extension (.pyd on Windows, .so on Linux). It is installed into the Python environment and imported as import pyfastchess. It owns everything performance-critical: board state, legal move generation, Zobrist hashing, the MCTS tree, and position caching. None of this crosses the Python/C++ boundary at inference time — the C++ tree drives selection internally and surfaces only the leaf nodes that need NN evaluation.

chessbot is the Python package (src/chessbot/ in src layout). It imports pyfastchess and owns the rest: neural network inference, training orchestration, selfplay loop, rescoring, game review, and configuration. The split is intentional — the Python side is meant to stay thin so that a future full-C++ inference path requires minimal rework.

docs.title: The Chess-Library Backend
docs.text:
The C++ board layer wraps Disservin's chess-library, a header-only C++20 library for board representation and move generation. Rather than exposing it directly to Python, pyfastchess presents it through a Backend facade defined in backend.hpp.

The facade exposes the operations Xerces actually uses:

  • board_to_64_tokens() — encodes the position as 64 int16 token IDs, one per square, in side-to-move-as-white orientation. This is the primary input to the neural network.
  • legal_move_mask() — returns a 4288-element uint8 mask and a (uci, flat_index) map. The 4288 slots correspond to the 64×67 policy logit layout (64 source squares × 67 destination slots, where the extra 3 slots per source handle underpromotions).
  • moves_to_indices() — converts a list of UCI strings to flat policy indices; used when inserting cached priors.
  • push_uci() / unmake() — make and unmake moves with full history for tree reuse.
  • hash() — incremental Zobrist key, used as the cache lookup key.
  • Terminal detection, check detection, and material counting are also exposed for adjudication.

The 64-token board encoding and the 4288-slot move space are defined entirely in C++ and are fixed across the whole stack. The Python side never encodes boards or computes move indices itself.

docs.title: Python/C++ Interface
docs.text:
pyfastchess is built with pybind11. The binding layer in binding.cpp exposes Board, MCTSTree, Cache, and supporting structs (WDL, ChildDetail, PVItem, CollectResults) as Python objects.

The critical hot-path interface is:

  1. Python calls tree.collect_many_leaves(n_new, n_fastpath) — C++ runs PUCT descent and returns new leaf nodes that need NN evaluation, plus counts of cache hits and terminals.
  2. Python runs batched NN inference on the leaf boards.
  3. Python calls tree.raw_cache_bulk_insert_np(zobrists, values, logits) to populate the raw policy cache, then tree.apply_result(node, priors, wdl) per leaf.

Everything between steps 1 and 3 — PUCT scoring, virtual loss, backpropagation, cache lookup — happens entirely in C++ with no Python overhead.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Both repos read from a shared Config object (src/chessbot/config.py) loaded from a YAML file at run start. Unknown keys raise AttributeError immediately rather than silently being ignored. The C++ tree receives its configuration through explicit setter calls (set_cpuct(), set_dirichlet(), set_vscale(), etc.) after the tree is constructed.

docs.title: Orchestration
docs.text:
scripts/run_selfplay.py <run_tag> starts a run. All of the run's long-lived state lives in one object, SelfPlayRunner (src/chessbot/selfplay_runner.py), whose main loop does everything on one thread, in order: reap and respawn dead workers, keep the game queue topped up, drain finished games into the rescorer, tick rescoring, and launch or poll a retrain.

Processes. The runner manages a small fleet:

  • xc0 workers: each runs child_looper() → GameLooper, playing many games concurrently with batched GPU inference.
  • lc0 worker: runs the LC0 teacher probes on its own queue (see Rescoring & Retraining).
  • Stockfish rescore threads: analyze finished games. One extra thread is added automatically while the rescore backlog is deep and retired once it clears.
  • Retrain worker: spawned fresh for each retrain and torn down afterwards.

One game queue. Selfplay games, validation games and blunder-replay probes all ride a single FIFO queue that every xc0 worker pulls from. At startup it is seeded in priority order: probes first (they're single-move, so Stockfish has work within seconds), then validation, then selfplay, filled deep enough to bring every worker slot up at once. Workers report finished games and telemetry back on their own queues, and receive pause, unpause and reload commands on a per-worker message queue.

Retrain boundary. When the primary buffer fills, the runner spawns the retrain worker, pauses selfplay once the worker is ready, and lets it train only after every worker has released the GPU. When training finishes, the runner re-reads the run's config (so edits take effect at each retrain boundary without a restart), rebuilds the TRT engine, and unpauses the fleet on the new weights. Validation batches and bulk BRP rounds are scheduled off the same retrain counter.

Unattended runs. scripts/run_selfplay_loop.py wraps the runner for long campaigns. It runs a tag to its game budget, iterates into the next tag (cloning its config), and relaunches on crashes, silent hangs or stalls, killing orphaned workers and engines first. It halts safely on repeated failures or low disk. An operator console on stdin (stop, pause/resume, worker and Stockfish scaling) stays available throughout.

The live telemetry view aggregates across all workers and updates each reporting interval. Key metrics: moves/sec (MPS) and leaf evaluations/sec (LPS) reflect game and NN throughput respectively; games/hour gives the effective data generation rate; cache hit rate shows what fraction of leaf collections were resolved by the C++ priors cache without NN inference; PUCT stats and per-scenario W/D/L breakdowns make it easy to spot if one game type is producing systematically lopsided results.

docs.title: GameLooper
docs.text:
GameLooper manages a pool of active_games (up to games_at_once concurrent ChessGame instances) and drives the inference loop. Every tree is registered with a single C++ MCTSForest, which owns leaf collection and board encoding across all games at once — the Python loop never touches individual leaf boards.

Each iteration:

  1. forest.resolve_all_inflight() — settle any leaves whose NN results arrived last iteration.
  2. For each active game, game.tree.collect_many_leaves(this_mbs, max_fastpath) gathers new leaf nodes that need NN evaluation. Cache hits and terminals are resolved in C++ and don't surface here. A per-game micro_batch sets the target leaf count; unused budget rolls into a bonus that lets the next game temporarily double its microbatch, keeping the aggregate batch full.
  3. batch_encoder() — one C++ call (forest.get_all_encoded, or get_all_lc0_features for the lc0_trt backend) returns (keys_np, enc_np): the zobrist keys and encoded boards for every pending leaf in the forest.
  4. format_and_predict(keys, enc) — the encoded batch is sliced into macro_batch chunks and run through infer(...), returning (policy_logits [B, 1858], wdl [B, 3]). raw_cache_bulk_insert_np(keys, wdl, logits) writes results into the C++ raw cache, where masking/softmax happen in build_priors.
  5. On the next iteration resolve_all_inflight() expands the waiting nodes and backpropagates.
  6. Games that reach a terminal state are popped from the forest, finalized (serialized to pickle and enqueued for rescoring), and removed from active_games; pull_from_queue() refills the pool.

The inference step is intentionally kept as the sole GPU operation. There is no per-game GPU work; encoding, cache lookups, and tree updates are all CPU-side C++, with Python only orchestrating.

Pause and reload. When the main process sends a pause signal, GameLooper tears down the inference session (del self.infer/del self.model), calls torch.cuda.empty_cache() for the PyTorch backends (the TRT backends need no explicit free), clears the priors cache, and blocks on the message queue until an unpause arrives. An unpause that arrives early is buffered so the wait can't deadlock. On resume it reloads the model from the path in the unpause message and rebuilds the inference function. VRAM is released before the retrain subprocess starts so both fit on the same GPU.

docs.title: StockfishThread
docs.text:
StockfishThread runs a Stockfish engine on a background daemon thread, handling positions that need engine evaluation during selfplay — primarily for games played against Stockfish and for the vs-SF validation rounds.

Games submit a (game_id, board_fen) pair via submit(). The thread drains its input queue, runs Stockfish to the configured depth, and pushes (game_id, result_tuple) to a response queue. The result tuple contains (eval_cp_stm_pov, best_move_uci, wdl_tuple). Games poll the response queue at the start of each move.

docs.title: Game Curriculum
docs.text:
GameGenerator selects starting positions according to a weighted scenario mix configured per run. The mix leans heavily on real openings: half of all games start from the initial position and most of the rest come from opening books and UHO, while the synthetic scenarios are a small minority. The active m137_8c8t curriculum is:

Scenario Weight Description startpos 50% Standard starting position UHO 24% Unbalanced Human Openings, white to move at ply 16 pre_opened 10% Longer opening lines (> 2 moves) pre_opened_mini 9% Short opening lines (<= 2 moves) random_init 3% Random legal position from the opening phase piece_odds 2% Material-unbalanced positions piece_training 2% Focused endgame piece training positions

UHO positions come from UHO_XXL_2022_+100_+129.pgn, a corpus of unbalanced human games. All UHO positions are white-to-move at ply 16, ensuring the engine sees non-trivial positions with varied pawn structures early in training.

docs.title: Game Adjudication
docs.text:
Games terminate on checkmate or draw by the rules, but several early-exit conditions are also active:

  • Eval collar — if one side's evaluation stays above a threshold for collar_n_consec consecutive moves, the game is adjudicated as a win for that side.
  • Eval draw — if all evaluations within a rolling window stay near zero, the game is adjudicated as a draw.
  • Max game length — hard cap to prevent runaway games.

Syzygy tablebase adjudication (<= 5 pieces) and material-diff cutoffs are also configurable per run. The adjudicator flags in effect for a game are recorded with its training data so rescoring knows how each outcome was reached.

docs.title: Bootstrap Data Pipeline
docs.text:
Before self-play begins, the model is pretrained on a large static dataset built from two sources. scripts/data/build_bootstrap_records.py is the canonical tool for this.

lc0 source — lc0 V6 binary training chunks decoded directly to xc0h tokens via v6_planes_to_xc0h (no float32 intermediate). Draws are dropped at 50%. 3 workers each drain a disjoint chunk subset.

xc0 source — Xerces selfplay game logs from historical run tags. For each game that passes a GAME_CPL_MAX=20 filter, plies with SF analysis loss <= MOVE_CPL_MAX=15 and tree search data are extracted. The board is replayed through board.history_tokens(K=6) via pyfastchess to produce the xc0h encoding, preserving full opening history via warm replay of the prefix. SF moves are skipped. 4 workers each handle a disjoint subset of run tags.

Both sources produce records with schema:

xc0h_board  int16[393]    K=6 history frames + meta tokens
policy      float32[1858] normalized visit distribution (no clipping)
wdl         float32[3]    Z_BLEND * result_wdl + (1-Z_BLEND) * search_wdl

Target is 20M records per source (40M total). Output goes to a staging directory, then a single shuffle pass via scripts/data/shuffle_xco.py produces the final training-ready shards.

docs.title: MateLock
docs.text: When a forced mate is found anywhere in the tree during backpropagation, Xerces locks the next visit through that mating line — bypassing PUCT entirely until the game ends or a non-mating solution is found. Simultaneously, children that lead to the engine losing receive a decaying penalty on their PUCT score to discourage revisiting them.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
During backprop, when a terminal node resolves as a win for the side to move, the parent records the winning move via an atomic compare-and-swap:

// on terminal win during backprop
if (stm_wins) {
    p->set_must_visit_uci(n->uci);
} else if (v_scalar != 0.0f) {
    n->performance_penalty.fetch_add(1);
}

set_must_visit_uci uses a three-state machine (0=empty, 2=writing, 1=ready) so only one thread wins the write under concurrent descent. On subsequent descents into that node, the forced move is checked before any PUCT scoring:

// selection — checked before PUCT
char forced_uci[16];
if (take_must_visit_uci(forced_uci)) {
    ++cc->count_must_visit;
    // walk directly to the mating child, no scoring
}

Losing children accumulate performance_penalty. Each time selection evaluates that child, the penalty is subtracted from its PUCT score and then decremented by one — decaying naturally as visits accumulate rather than permanently suppressing the move.

int pen = ch->performance_penalty.load();
if (pen > 0) {
    score -= static_cast<float>(pen);
    ch->performance_penalty.fetch_sub(1);
}

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: The side that would deliver mate is forced to replay the moves leading to checkmate and the side the would lose via checkmate is encouraged to keep trying other moves to avoid losing. This effectively creates a forced checkmate test. If its possible for one side to force-checkmate the other, this feature will find it.

docs.title: Robust Selection Criteria
docs.text: Robust Selection Criteria (RSC) is an alternative to pure visit-count move selection. Rather than always playing the most-visited move, RSC scores each candidate using a weighted ensemble of five signals and selects the move with the strongest combined case. It is used both for final move selection and as a component of early stopping.

docs.title: The Five Signals
docs.text:
RSC considers the top-N candidates (up to 5, minimum 100 visits each). For each, it collects:

  • Visit count — raw simulation visits
  • Q — mean action value (white-POV, flipped for black)
  • Qema — exponential moving average of Q, smoothing out noisy early estimates (span configurable via qema_span)
  • Visit share — EMA of how frequently this child was selected relative to siblings during search
  • Qdelta_sign — EMA of the sign of Q deltas relative to the side to move; positive means Q has been trending in the current player's favor (span configurable via qdelta_span)

Each signal is min-max normalized to [0, 1] across the candidate set, then converted to a probability distribution. The final RSC score is an equal-weight sum:

const float w = 0.2f;
float score = w*p_vis[i] + w*p_q[i] + w*p_qe[i] + w*p_vs[i] + w*p_ds[i];

docs.title: Move Selection
docs.text:
RSC is activated above a configurable sim threshold (robust_only_above). Below that threshold, Xerces falls back to most-visited. When RSC is active, only candidates with at least min(most_visits * 0.7, 2000) visits are eligible — moves that haven't been explored enough to form a reliable estimate are excluded regardless of their score.

visit_threshold = min(most_visits * 0.7, 2000)
best_uci = max(
    (d.uci for d in details if d.N >= visit_threshold and d.uci in rsc),
    key=lambda u: rsc[u]
)

docs.title: Why Not Just Most-Visited
docs.text: A move that accumulates a large visit lead early can be difficult to surpass within the remaining sim budget, even if a better move emerges later. RSC requires multiple independent signals to agree — a move wins the vote only if it's well-visited and has a good value and that value has been stable.

docs.title: SmartGate
docs.text:
SmartGate is a suppress-only policy gate. Xerces scores moves with a relational from/to head: two attention towers whose dot products score every source-destination pair. That head is good at geometry (which moves are plausible given piece placement), but it has no cheap way to say "this specific move is wrong here", whether that means illegal in this exact position or a known bad idea. SmartGate is a second, parallel pathway whose only job is to shut moves the from/to head over-weights. It can never invent a move the from/to head didn't already like.

It is live in the active m137_8c8t model. See the neural network page for where it sits in the full architecture.

docs.title: Its Own Accumulators
docs.text: The trunk carries 8 global accumulator tokens appended to the 64 board squares. SmartGate reads two of them concatenated: a private token (67) that nothing else reads, and a token (68) it shares with both policy towers. The private register lets it learn a representation tuned for vetoing moves. The shared one ties it to what the policy head is attending to.

docs.title: The Gate
docs.text:
The 512-d accumulator pair goes through a GELU feed-forward with a residual and norm, then a linear layer to one shut-logit per move over the 1858 "sometimes-legal" move domain:

gi       = cat(x[:, 67], x[:, 68])                     # 2 accumulators, 512-d
g        = gate_norm(gi + gate_ff2(gelu(gate_ff1(gi))))
gate_raw = gate_out(g)                                 # [B, 1858] shut-logits
policy   = move_logits - scale * sigmoid(gate_raw)

Because scale * sigmoid(.) >= 0, the gate can only ever subtract from a move's logit. It has no additive branch: a move the from/to head scores low stays low, and the gate cannot rescue it.

Two learnable knobs bound how hard it can push. Both are clamped after every optimizer step:

  • Per-move bias, held in [0, 5]: each of the 1858 slots has its own baseline openness.
  • Global scale, held in [0, 12]: the maximum logit penalty the gate can apply.

docs.title: Weak at Init, Earns Its Scale
docs.text: The per-move bias starts at 4.0 (sigmoid(4) ≈ 0.98, mostly shut) and the scale starts at 1.0. At init the gate therefore subtracts a near-uniform ~1 from every move, which softmax ignores, and the from/to head's priors pass through effectively untouched. The scale only grows as the gate learns to tell moves apart, so it can't destabilize a policy head that hasn't learned anything yet.

docs.title: Supervised on Legality
docs.text:
SmartGate isn't left to discover its job from the policy loss alone. It gets its own objective: a binary cross-entropy on gate_raw predicting whether each of the 1858 moves is illegal in the current position. Any move the policy target gives visits to counts as legal, since every legal move carries a one-visit floor. Legal moves are up-weighted so the rare "keep open" class isn't drowned out. The gate loss is held at a small fixed share of the main policy + value loss, and its share shrinks once it is well trained, so a converged gate stops competing with the main objective.

The result is a learned, position-specific legality mask that keeps policy mass off impossible moves. On top of that, the policy loss still flows through the gate, so it remains free to shut legal moves the from/to head systematically over-rates.

docs.title: Why Suppress-Only
docs.text: An additive gate could quietly become a second, redundant policy head, competing with the from/to towers and muddying which pathway is responsible for a prediction. Constraining it to subtraction forces a clean division of labor: the from/to head proposes, the gate disposes. It also matches the failure modes it targets. Illegal moves and confidently wrong moves both call for suppression; neither needs a second voice proposing new moves.

docs.title: Prior Temperature Scaling
docs.text: After priors are built for a node (softmax, uniform_eps blending, prior_clip_max clamping), Xerces optionally sharpens them further if the resulting distribution is still too spread out. The intuition: a high-entropy prior over legal moves — several moves rated near-equally plausible — is a weak signal for PUCT to explore with, even when the position itself is not actually balanced. Sharpening toward a target entropy gives search a clearer starting point without hand-picking a move.

docs.title: When It Fires
docs.text:
Two gates control activation, both config-driven and off by default:

if (tempscale_entropy_target_ > 0.0f && k >= 5.0f && q_stm >= tempscale_trigger_q_) {
  • tempscale_entropy_target (0 = disabled) — the normed-entropy ceiling; distributions already below it are left alone.
  • tempscale_trigger_q — a STM-POV Q floor (-2 = always eligible, 0.5 = only sharpen when already winning).
  • At least 5 legal moves — not worth the search for near-forced positions.

docs.title: Binary Search on Temperature
docs.text:
If the node's normed entropy exceeds the target, Xerces binary-searches for the sharpening exponent that lands closest to the target without ever increasing entropy:

float lo = 0.3f, hi = 1.0f, best = 0.75f, best_dist = 1e30f;

for (int iter = 0; iter < 5; ++iter) {
    const float mid = (lo + hi) * 0.5f;
    const float inv_mid = 1.0f / mid;
    // raw_prior ** (1/mid), renormalize, re-blend uniform_eps + prior_clip_max, recompute entropy
    ...
    if (ne_mid < ne) {
        const float dist = std::abs(ne_mid - tempscale_entropy_target_);
        if (dist < best_dist) { best = mid; best_dist = dist; }
        if (dist < 0.05f) break;
    }
    if (ne_mid < tempscale_entropy_target_) lo = mid;
    else hi = mid;
}

Five iterations, bounds [0.3, 1.0] on the temperature T (exponent applied is 1/T, so the search only ever sharpens, never flattens). A candidate is only accepted as best if it actually reduced entropy relative to the untouched distribution — a candidate that overshoots back up is rejected even if its distance to the target looks close. The final chosen temperature is reapplied through the same pipeline (raw prior power, renormalize, uniform_eps blend, prior_clip_max clamp) so the sharpened distribution obeys the same invariants as any other prior.

docs.title: Relationship to the Rescorer's Version
docs.text: The same target-entropy/bisection shape is used a second time, independently, in Rescorer/build_bootstrap_records.py on the Python side — there it reshapes the final MCTS visit distribution into a policy training target (gated on zero centipawn loss and enough legal moves), not the root prior before search even starts. The two serve different purposes and are configured separately: this page is about the live, in-search C++ version gated by tempscale_entropy_target/tempscale_trigger_q.

docs.title: VScale
docs.text: VScale compresses NN value estimates during backpropagation while letting terminal outcomes propagate at full strength. The idea is that true terminal states with value e.g. (1, 0, 0) are difficult to distinquish from "completely winning" NN evals e.g. (0.99, 0.01, 0.0). Downscaling NN values allows true terminals to stand out better and influence search more effectively.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
During backprop, the scalar used to update W (the accumulator for Q) is scaled by vscale for NN-evaluated nodes and left at full power for terminals:

const float v_scalar = (wdl.win - wdl.loss) * (is_terminal ? 1.0f : vscale_);
...
n->W += v_scalar;
n->Q = n->W / static_cast<float>(n->visit_count());

Only W and Q are affected. The p_win, p_draw, p_loss accumulators always receive the full WDL — so the tree's WDL statistics remain uncompressed. VScale only affects the value signal that PUCT uses for move selection.

At vscale=1.0 the behavior is standard. Values below 1.0 flatten Q differences between children, making visit counts carry more relative weight in selection. Values above 1.0 amplify the value signal. The active config uses vscale=0.9.

docs.title: What is Xerces?
docs.text:
Xerces is an open-source, neural-network powered chess engine, trained on multiple data sources: published Lc0 game data, curated Xerces self-play data, and ongoing self-play with Stockfish rescoring.

  • Monte Carlo Tree Search with PUCT selection
  • Neural network evaluation (an 8-conv + 8-transformer "m137_8c8t" model, ~18.4M params)
  • Stockfish post-hoc rescoring for blunder detection and visit redistribution
  • Async retrain loop running between self-play rounds

The Python package handles training, search orchestration, and inference in PyTorch, served through ONNX Runtime with TensorRT. It sits on top of a high-performance C++ backend built on Disservin's chess-library, which provides the core board representation, move generation, and MCTS tree.

docs.title: Design Philosophy
docs.text:
Xerces is built around the idea that chess strength emerges from the interaction between search and learning, not from neural scale alone.

Rather than pursuing the largest possible networks, Xerces explores whether moderately-sized, information-dense models paired with aggressive, adaptive search can produce strong and interesting play under real compute constraints.

The project emphasizes:

  • search as a first-class intelligence system
  • efficient information flow through priors
  • empirical refinement during search
  • runtime adaptability
  • systems-level optimization over benchmark chasing

Xerces treats the neural network as a powerful guide, not an oracle. The search process itself is viewed as an active computational partner capable of reshaping, amplifying, and stress-testing learned beliefs in real time.

Part of the appeal is the constraint itself. Xerces is developed and trained entirely on a single consumer GPU (RTX 2080, 8GB VRAM, i9-9700K) as a non-commercial project. Running on cloud compute or a multi-GPU cluster is a deliberate non-goal. The interesting engineering challenge is doing more with less, and the design decisions throughout the stack reflect that.

docs.title: Engine Landscape
docs.text: Chess engines have gone through a few distinct eras. Xerces sits in the most recent one.

docs.title: Deep Blue
docs.text: Deep Blue was IBM's purpose-built chess supercomputer that defeated Garry Kasparov in 1997. It represented the apex of handcrafted, hardware-accelerated alpha-beta search — evaluation functions written by grandmasters, tuned by engineers, running on custom VLSI chips. Deep Blue was a landmark achievement, but it was also a dead end: the knowledge was bespoke, brittle, and non-transferable.

docs.title: Stockfish
docs.text: Stockfish is the dominant open-source classical engine and the gold standard for raw playing strength in the alpha-beta lineage. Classical engines like Stockfish work by searching a game tree with alpha-beta pruning — exhaustively evaluating positions to a fixed depth, using handcrafted (and later, NNUE-learned) evaluation to score leaf nodes. Stockfish is extraordinarily strong, but its search is fundamentally bounded by depth: it knows what it can see, and no further.

docs.title: AlphaZero
docs.text: DeepMind's AlphaZero paper (2017) changed the picture entirely. AlphaZero replaced alpha-beta search with Monte Carlo Tree Search guided by a neural network trained purely through self-play — no handcrafted evaluation, no opening books, no endgame tablebases. It learned chess from scratch in hours and surpassed Stockfish. The key insight was that a strong policy and value network can focus search on the most promising lines, making deep alpha-beta exhaustiveness unnecessary.

docs.title: Leela Chess Zero
docs.text: Leela Chess Zero (Lc0) is the open-source community implementation of the AlphaZero approach. It proved the method generalizes beyond DeepMind's compute budget — with enough self-play games and a community of contributors, an open project could reach superhuman strength using the same MCTS + neural network paradigm. Lc0 has beaten Stockfish in top computer chess competition, winning TCEC Season 15 and Season 17. Lc0 is Xerces's closest conceptual ancestor and an ongoing reference point for comparison.

docs.title: How Does it Work?
docs.text:
Xerces is a neural-network-guided MCTS chess engine. Like AlphaZero and Leela Chess Zero, it works by having a model supply priors over legal moves, then using search to test those beliefs against actual continuations.

The short version is:

  1. The model looks at a chess position.
  2. It predicts which moves look promising and who is likely winning.
  3. MCTS uses those predictions to build a search tree.
  4. The search repeatedly explores, expands, evaluates, and backs up results.
  5. The engine plays the move that survives the most search pressure.
  6. The resulting search data becomes training data for the next model.

docs.title: MCTS 101
docs.text:
Monte Carlo Tree Search is a way to make decisions by building a tree of possible future positions. Each node in the tree is a board position. Each edge is a legal move. The root is the current position.

For each simulation, MCTS does four things:

  1. Select a path through the existing tree.
  2. Expand a new position that has not been searched yet.
  3. Evaluate that position with the neural network.
  4. Back up the result through every node on the selected path.

Over many simulations, good moves tend to collect more visits. Bad moves may still be checked, but they receive less attention unless there is a reason to look again.

This is different from a traditional alpha-beta engine like Stockfish. Stockfish uses a shallow NN evaluation and extremely fast but relatively unguided tactical search. Xerces instead uses a neural network evaluation and a search process that behaves more like progressive evidence gathering.

docs.title: What the Neural Network Predicts
docs.text:
The model produces two outputs.

The first is policy. Policy is a probability distribution over moves. It tells MCTS which moves look promising before the search has spent much time on them.

The second is value. Value is the model's estimate of the position. Xerces uses a win/draw/loss head — rather than a single scalar, the model returns three probabilities from the side-to-move perspective that sum to 1.

So when the model evaluates a position, it returns something like:

policy: e4 28%, d4 22%, Nf3 12%, c4 10%, ...
value:  W 45%  D 38%  L 17%

The model is called at every new node in the tree — not just the root. Each time the search expands a position it hasn't seen before, the network evaluates it and returns a fresh set of priors and a WDL estimate for that specific position. This is how the policy adapts as the game progresses.

The model gives the search a starting point. Those values are then tested by repeatedly running the expand, evaluate, and back up loop.

docs.title: How PUCT Guides the Search
docs.text:
PUCT is the selection formula used by AlphaZero-style MCTS engines. It balances two competing forces:

  • Exploitation: search moves that already look good.
  • Exploration: search moves that the model thinks may be promising, even if they have not been visited much yet.

Each candidate move receives a score at every selection step:

Q is the running average value from previous visits — it rises if a move keeps leading to good positions, falls if it doesn't. U is the exploration bonus: proportional to the policy prior and inversely proportional to visit count, so high-prior moves get early attention but that bonus shrinks as visits stack up.

The search repeatedly chooses the move with the highest Q + U score. Early in the search, policy matters a lot. Later in the search, accumulated evidence matters more.

docs.title: One Simulation Step
docs.text:
A single Xerces simulation looks roughly like this:

start at root
while current node is already expanded:
    choose child with best PUCT score
    move to that child

evaluate the new leaf position with the neural network
create child nodes using the policy output
back up the value through the selected path

During backup, the evaluated value updates visit counts and average values along the path. Because chess alternates sides, the value is flipped as it moves from one player's perspective to the other.

After thousands of simulations, the root node contains a visit distribution over legal moves. The most-visited move is usually the move Xerces plays.

docs.title: Why Visits Matter
docs.text:
The visit count is important because it represents search confidence. A move can look good after one evaluation and still collapse after deeper exploration. A move that attracts thousands of visits has survived more pressure.

This is also why MCTS produces useful training targets. The model does not only learn from the final game result. It learns from the search distribution itself. If MCTS spends most of its time on one move, the next model is trained to assign that move a higher prior in similar positions.

That creates the core improvement loop:

better model -> better search -> better training targets -> better model

docs.title: Pretraining
docs.text:
Before self-play begins, the model is pretrained on static data. This gives it basic chess structure before it has to generate its own training data.

Pretraining can include positions analyzed by Stockfish, published Lc0 data, existing Xc0 game data, or other supervised targets. The goal is not to make a perfect engine immediately. The goal is to reduce the amount of self-play training required.

A randomly initialized model gives weak priors and noisy values. Search can still run, but it wastes a lot of effort. A pretrained model gives the search better first guesses, which makes self-play refinement much more efficient.

docs.title: Self-Play Refinement
docs.text:
After pretraining, Xerces improves through self-play.

In self-play, Xerces plays games against itself. For every move, it stores the position, the final search visit distribution, and eventually the game result. Those records become training examples.

A simplified training row looks like this:

position: board state before the move
policy target: MCTS visit distribution
value target: game outcome or refined value target

The policy target teaches the model to imitate the search. The value target teaches the model which positions are actually converting into wins, losses, or draws.

After enough games are collected, the model is retrained. Then the updated model plays more self-play games, generating a stronger batch of data. The cycle repeats.

docs.title: Training Mode vs Competition Mode
docs.text: Xerces behaves differently depending on whether it is generating training data or trying to play the strongest possible move.

docs.title: Training Mode
docs.text:
In training mode, the goal is not only to win the current game. The goal is to produce useful data.

Training mode may use more randomness, exploration, sampling, or noise. This helps the engine see a wider range of positions instead of repeating the same lines forever.

The engine records search distributions, results, metadata, and later rescoring information. These outputs are more important than a single game's result, because they feed the next training cycle.

Training mode is designed to be curious.

docs.title: Competition Mode
docs.text:
In competition mode, the goal is simple: play the strongest move available.

Competition mode reduces randomness and uses the search result more directly. The engine usually chooses the most robust move from the root search, often the move with the strongest visit count or best final selection score.

Exploration still exists inside the search through PUCT, but the final move choice is much more deterministic. The engine is no longer trying to create broad training data. It is trying to convert the current position.

Competition mode is designed to be ruthless.

docs.title: Validation Mode
docs.text: Validation mode is used to measure how strong the engine has become. Xerces plays a set of test games from fixed opening positions, scored against a reference opponent, usually Stockfish at a fixed depth. The result is a pass/fail score that determines whether the engine has improved enough to advance to the next difficulty level.
